1.summary: Yahweh insists that he has loved Israel, then rebukes the priests for offering blind, lame and sick animals on his altar, despising the God whose name is great among the nations.
1.lookfor: Notice the pattern of God's statement, the people's question, and God's answer, and what the priests are bringing to the altar.

names.name: Malachi
names.gloss: The prophet, or a title meaning my messenger.

names.name: Esau
names.gloss: Jacob's twin brother and ancestor of the Edomites.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: The land south-east of the Dead Sea, home of Esau's descendants.

insights.title: Yet you say
insights.body: Malachi is built from about six disputes. God makes a statement (I have loved you), the people object (How have you loved us?), and God answers (1:2). The pattern repeats with each charge. It reveals a community that questions God at every turn.

insights.title: Loved Jacob, hated Esau
insights.body: I loved Jacob; but Esau I hated (1:2-3). In covenant language, love and hate often mean choose and not choose, rather than emotions. Paul quotes the verse in Romans 9 to speak of God's free choice. Readers have long debated whether it concerns nations or individuals, and history or eternal destiny.

insights.title: Edom's ruin
insights.body: Edom says it will rebuild its ruins (1:4). By Malachi's day, Arab tribes such as the Nabataeans had pushed the Edomites out of their homeland, and Edom never recovered. For Judah, struggling under Persian rule, Edom's fall was a sign that God still cared for them.

insights.title: Blind and lame sacrifices
insights.body: The law required sacrificial animals to be without defect. The priests were accepting blind, lame and sick animals (1:8), giving God what was cheapest. Malachi asks whether the Persian governor would accept such a gift.

insights.title: Shut the doors
insights.body: God wishes someone would shut the temple doors so that no more useless fires would be lit on the altar (1:10). Better no worship than empty worship. Isaiah and Amos make similar complaints.

insights.title: A pure offering everywhere
insights.body: From the rising of the sun to its setting, God's name is great among the nations, and in every place incense and a pure offering are brought (1:11). Jewish interpreters have read this of prayer offered by Jews scattered abroad, or of sincere worship among Gentiles. Early Christian writers and Catholic tradition applied it to the Eucharist offered among all nations.

insights.title: What a weariness
insights.body: The priests sniff at the altar and say, Behold, what a weariness it is! (1:13). Their problem is boredom with God more than open rebellion. Worship has become a chore.

insights.title: A father and master
insights.body: If I am a father, then where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is the respect due me? (1:6). The priests call God Lord but act as if he does not matter. What might honouring God look like in the ordinary details of life and worship?

2.summary: Yahweh warns the priests who have corrupted the covenant with Levi, then rebukes the people for marrying worshippers of foreign gods and for divorcing the wives of their youth, and for doubting God's justice.
2.lookfor: Notice the ideal priest described in 2:5-7, the appeal to one father in 2:10, and what God says about marriage in 2:14-16.

names.name: Levi
names.gloss: Jacob's son, ancestor of the priestly tribe.

insights.title: Dung on their faces
insights.body: God threatens to spread the dung of their feasts on the priests' faces (2:3). The dung and entrails of sacrificed animals were carried outside the camp and burned. To be smeared with it would make the priests unclean and unfit for service.

insights.title: The covenant with Levi
insights.body: God's covenant with Levi was of life and peace (2:5). This may recall the covenant of peace given to Phinehas, or Moses's blessing on Levi, whose task was to teach Israel the law. The faithful priest is a messenger of Yahweh (2:7).

insights.title: The priest's lips
insights.body: The priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth (2:7). Priests were not only sacrificers but teachers. Malachi faults them for causing many to stumble and for showing favouritism in their rulings (2:8-9).

insights.title: Married to foreign gods
insights.body: Judah has married the daughter of a foreign god (2:11), meaning women who worshipped other gods. Ezra and Nehemiah faced the same problem, worried that such marriages would bring idolatry into the community. The concern is religious faithfulness, as the phrase foreign god shows, rather than ethnicity.

insights.title: Tears on the altar
insights.body: The people cover the altar with tears because God no longer accepts their offerings (2:13). The reason, God says, is that they have betrayed the wife of their youth (2:14). Faithlessness at home affects worship.

insights.title: The wife of your covenant
insights.body: Yahweh is witness between you and the wife of your youth ... your companion, and the wife of your covenant (2:14). Marriage is presented as a covenant before God, not just a private contract. The word for companion means a partner, an equal.

insights.title: I hate divorce
insights.body: For I hate divorce (2:16) is the traditional translation, but the Hebrew is notoriously difficult. Some modern versions read it as he who hates and divorces covers his garment with violence. Either way, the verse condemns men discarding their wives. Jesus later teaches strongly against divorce.

insights.title: One father
insights.body: Don't we all have one father? Hasn't one God created us? (2:10). Malachi grounds faithfulness to one another in having one Creator. If people share one Father, how should that change the way they treat each other?

3.summary: Yahweh promises a messenger to prepare his way and his sudden coming as a refiner, calls the people to return by bringing the full tithe, and records in a book of memory those who fear him.
3.lookfor: Notice the two messengers in 3:1, the images for the coming Lord, the challenge about tithes, and what happens when the faithful talk together.

names.name: Jacob
names.gloss: The people of Israel, called sons of Jacob.

names.name: Levi
names.gloss: The priestly tribe, here the priests and Levites.

insights.title: My messenger
insights.body: Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me (3:1). Mark opens his Gospel by combining this verse with Isaiah 40, and Jesus applies it to John the Baptist. In Hebrew my messenger is malachi, the name of the book.

insights.title: Refiner and launderer
insights.body: Who can endure the day of his coming? For he is like a refiner's fire, and like launderers' soap (3:2). Refining melts away impurities from metal; launderers scrubbed cloth with strong alkali. The Lord's coming will purify, beginning with the priests (3:3). Handel set these verses to music in Messiah.

insights.title: Judgment on oppression
insights.body: God will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, and those who cheat workers of wages and deny justice to widows, orphans and foreigners (3:5). The day of the Lord answers the complaint Where is the God of justice? (2:17).

insights.title: I don't change
insights.body: I, Yahweh, don't change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed (3:6). Israel survived only because God's commitment did not waver. James speaks of the Father of lights with whom there is no variation.

insights.title: Robbing God
insights.body: Will a man rob God? ... In tithes and offerings (3:8). Tithes of produce supported the Levites and the poor. Nehemiah found the Levites had left the temple because the tithes had not been brought.

insights.title: Test me
insights.body: Bring the whole tithe ... and test me now in this ... if I will not open you the windows of heaven (3:10). Elsewhere testing God is forbidden; this is a rare invitation to put God's promise to the proof. Windows of heaven recalls the flood, now opened for blessing.

insights.title: A book of memory
insights.body: When those who feared Yahweh spoke together, God listened and a book of memory was written (3:16). Persian kings kept records of those who had served them, as in Esther. God remembers the faithful, who will be his own possession (3:17).

insights.title: Is it vain to serve God?
insights.body: Some said, It is vain to serve God (3:14), since the proud seem to prosper. The faithful answer not by argument but by speaking together and fearing God (3:16). How does a community keep faith when cynicism seems justified?

4.summary: The coming day will burn up the wicked like stubble, but the sun of righteousness will rise with healing for those who fear God; the book closes by calling Israel to remember the law of Moses and promising Elijah before the great day.
4.lookfor: Notice the two outcomes of the day, the image of the sun with wings, and the two figures named in the last three verses.

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Another name for Mount Sinai, where God gave the law.

names.name: Elijah
names.gloss: The 9th-century BC prophet who was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind.

insights.title: Root and branch
insights.body: The day burns like a furnace, leaving the wicked neither root nor branch (4:1). The phrase root and branch has entered English for complete removal. The same day brings opposite outcomes for the proud and for those who fear God.

insights.title: The sun with wings
insights.body: The sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings (4:2). The winged sun disk was a common symbol of divine power in Egyptian, Assyrian and Persian art, and it appears on royal seals from Judah. Malachi uses the image for God's saving justice. Charles Wesley's carol Hark! The Herald Angels Sing applies it to Christ.

insights.title: Calves let out
insights.body: You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall (4:2). Calves kept in a stall bound outside when released. Salvation is pictured as joyful freedom, not only rescue from judgment.

insights.title: Moses and Elijah
insights.body: The book ends by naming Moses and the law (4:4) and Elijah the prophet (4:5), representing the Law and the Prophets. On the mountain of Transfiguration, Moses and Elijah appear talking with Jesus.

insights.title: Elijah must come first
insights.body: God will send Elijah before the great and terrible day of Yahweh (4:5). Elijah never died but was taken up in a whirlwind, so his return was expected. The angel tells Zechariah that John will go in the spirit and power of Elijah, and Jesus identifies John as the Elijah who was to come.

insights.title: A cup for Elijah
insights.body: At the Passover meal, many Jewish families pour a cup for Elijah and open the door for him, expressing hope for his coming before the Messiah. Jewish tradition also gives Elijah the task of settling unresolved questions of law. The end of Malachi is read in synagogues on the Sabbath before Passover.

insights.title: Fathers and children
insights.body: Elijah will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the children to the fathers (4:6). Reconciliation between generations comes before the day of the Lord. When this book is read in synagogues, verse 5 is repeated after verse 6 so that the reading does not end on the word curse.

insights.title: The end of the Old Testament
insights.body: In Christian Bibles Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament, and its promise of Elijah leads straight into the Gospels and John the Baptist. In the Hebrew Bible, the Prophets end with Malachi but the canon ends with Chronicles. Either way, the prophetic books close looking forward to God's coming.

intro.who: The book is credited to Malachi, which means my messenger. It is unclear whether this was the prophet's name or a title taken from 3:1; the Greek translation reads his messenger, and an Aramaic Targum identifies the author with Ezra.
intro.when: The temple has been rebuilt and a Persian governor rules Judah, and the problems it addresses match those Nehemiah faced, so most scholars date it to the mid-5th century BC, around 470 to 430 BC.
intro.why: Through a series of disputes with a weary and cynical community, it calls priests and people back to wholehearted worship, faithfulness in marriage, justice and honest giving, and promises a messenger and the day of Yahweh that will refine and heal.

outline.title: The messenger, the tithe, the book
